places.name: La Padrona

famous.why: The signature pasta: silky ribbons in Parmigiano cream and black pepper, finished with a line of 12-year balsamico; every critic singles it out.
Oyster-infused vodka with sherry and a mignonette note, served with a little dish of pickles; the bar's calling card.
Unmolded at the table, wobbly and boozy; reviewers say save room for it.
A custardy, farinata-style skillet bread with a crisp bottom; a cozy starter critics push alongside the breads.
Eater's must-try: handkerchief pasta with a gentle milk-braised rabbit ragu, called one of the best pastas in town.

tips: Set an alarm for 9 AM ET exactly 14 days ahead; prime weekend slots go fast.
No reservation? The first-floor bar and lounge are walk-in only; arrive near opening.
Ask for a 'Club Room (Quiet Dining)' table if you want to talk; the main room is loud.
Order the tagliatelle for the table even if you get other pastas; pair with the martini list (Birth of Venus).

difficulty.why: Eater/Boston Magazine best-new-restaurant winner and Michelin-recommended; prime times sell out soon after the 14-day release, though bar walk-ins help.

warnings: Dining room is very lively and loud (the restaurant says so itself).
Expensive: pastas mid-$30s, mains $40-$50+; parties add up quickly.
Rabbit fazzoletti and seasonal antipasti rotate; tagliatelle is on the current menu ($34) but others may not be.

places.name: Sarma

famous.why: Sweet-spicy harissa-glazed duck, the longest-running crowd favorite and the go-to hearty plate (currently with carrot brown butter and fried almonds).
Warm za'atar flatbread that Time Out calls the no-brainer opener; cheap and always on the menu.
A playful meze with feta queso and tzatziki that Infatuation names as a favorite.
Spiced lamb patties on small buns with tomato butter and pickles; pictured in Infatuation's review.

tips: Walk-in plan: line up just before the 5 PM opening for one of the 20 bar seats (Eater and Infatuation both advise this).
Servers circulate trays of off-menu specials dim-sum style; anything you take is added to the bill.
Plates are small and priced individually; 2-3 per person is plenty, and the tab climbs fast.
Nearest T: Gilman Square (Green Line E); don't use the private lot next door.

difficulty.why: Infatuation lists it among America's toughest reservations; the 30-day Resy window at 10 AM sells out, so bar walk-ins at 5 PM are the realistic fallback.

warnings: Menu changes often (last updated 11/12/26); a specific dish may rotate off.
Cannot accommodate allium, spice, honey, nightshade, capsaicin or olive-oil allergies; no modifications.
Loud and tight when busy.
Closed Dec 24-28 and Jan 1.

places.name: Mooncusser

famous.why: The whole point: a short, choose-your-own tasting menu (two options per course plus snacks) that is rewritten every six weeks or so.

evidence.source: Boston Magazine (Best of Boston: tasting menu)

famous.why: Cod lacquered and paired with mango pickle and papadam; the dish both Michelin and Infatuation used to show off the kitchen's global seafood style.
Michelin calls the list and pairing well chosen and fairly priced; it's $75 on top of the menu.
Smoked trout with crispy tortilla bits and a sharp salsa verde, an Infatuation highlight from a recent menu.

tips: Each course offers two choices, so a pair can order different options and taste the whole menu.
Want a cheaper or more casual taste? Moon Bar on the street level is a la carte and books separately on OpenTable.
Get your garage ticket stamped by the host for the validated 10 St. James rate.

difficulty.why: Top-25 on Infatuation and Eater 38, but the tasting format and price keep it bookable on OpenTable with some notice; weekends need a week or two.

warnings: Menu changes about every six weeks; specific dishes (cod, trout) are likely gone. The current autumn menu lists bluefin tartare, hiramasa crudo, halibut stew and venison.
Dinner only, Tuesday-Saturday; closed Sunday-Monday.
Tasting menu only upstairs; no a la carte in the dining room.

places.name: Mahaniyom

famous.why: Shatteringly crisp fried chicken skins, the bar snack everyone orders.
Fiery red crab curry over delicate rice noodles; widely called the signature.
Three-spice fried pork cheeks, a drinking-food standout.
Pad Thai made with papaya strands instead of noodles; lightly sweet.
Signature Sazerac with Thai-tea-infused rye from a Michelin-noted cocktail program.

tips: Order family style: roughly 5-6 small plates for two to three people.
Check the chalkboard specials (e.g., oysters with chili jam).
Sister bar Merai down the block is open until 1 AM for after-dinner drinks.
2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand plus an Exceptional Cocktails award.

difficulty.why: Very small room and Bib Gourmand buzz; weekends need advance OpenTable booking, weeknights easier.

warnings: Closed Tuesdays.
Portions are small; plan on several plates.
Cocktail and seasonal fruit-salad menus change often.

places.name: Field & Vine

famous.why: Daily oysters with mignonette are the reliable opener; reviewers say to get shellfish on ice for the table.
Bright raw-fish plates (lately black bass aguachile and tuna tostadas) that Infatuation calls a constant.
The wood-fired Argentine grill in the open kitchen is the signature, and weekend steak specials show it off best.
Fire-blistered cabbage with spicy black garlic crema, brown butter and crispy rice, a vegetable dish critics single out.

tips: Order a few plates at a time and add as you go; the menu is built for sharing.
Ask about the tasting-menu option if you want the kitchen to choose.
Union Square parking is tight; take the Green Line (Union Square) or a ride share.
The restaurant is down an alley between Bronwyn and The Independent.

difficulty.why: Small room and an Infatuation Top 25 pick, so weekend primetime goes early on Resy, but weeknights are usually gettable.

warnings: Menu changes frequently; the cabbage and specific crudos may not be on. Steak specials are weekend-only.
2-hour table limit from your booked time; incomplete parties are not seated.
Closed Sunday and Monday.

places.name: Comfort Kitchen

famous.why: The breakout dish: nigella-crusted, butter-seared okra over garam masala yogurt that converts okra skeptics.
Jerk-spiced duck leg confit with rice, beans and Haitian pikliz; the main most often recommended (now also served as jerk-maple duck drumettes).
House signature built on baobab, ginger, orange and white tea; bright and easy-drinking.
Monkfish in a coconut curry broth, cited by Eater as a standout of the spice-route cooking.

tips: Book on OpenTable; reservations are effectively required at this 30-seat room, especially weekends.
No reservation: try the 6 bar stools or the patios (weather permitting) right at 4:30 PM.
Sunday brunch is easier to get and made OpenTable's Top 100 brunch list.
Street parking on Columbia Rd; Upham's Corner commuter rail and buses stop nearby.

difficulty.why: NYT Top 50 and Eater 38 alum in a tiny room; weekends book out days ahead, but weeknights and brunch are usually available.

warnings: Menu rotates (currently Dinner Menu #004): the current menu lists jerk duck drumettes and a prawn curry instead of the roasted duck leg and monkfish curry critics described.
Strict fees: $25/person late-cancellation and $10/guest same-day changes.
Closed Monday and Tuesday.
Automatic 20% gratuity for parties of 5+.

places.name: Neptune Oyster

famous.why: A huge, overflowing roll on toasted brioche, served hot and buttered or cold with mayo; one of Boston's most famous lobster rolls.
The daily list of East and West Coast oysters on the mirror behind the bar; order a mix from both coasts.
Salt pork and thyme chowder that Eater calls near-perfect.
Cheddar burger crowned with fried oysters and garlic mayo, a surf-and-turf cult order.

tips: Infatuation's trick: show up around 3 PM on a weekday to minimize (or skip) the line.
Put your name in and wander the North End; they'll call or text when a seat opens.
Bar seats turn fastest for 1-2 people.
Check the day-of-week specials (e.g., Monday lobster spaghettini, Saturday paella sarda).

difficulty.why: No reservations at all; prime-time waits commonly run 1-2 hours, but off-peak afternoons are manageable.

warnings: Walk-in only; expect a line outside, including in winter.
Lobster roll is market price and expensive.
Tiny, cramped room; not good for large groups or strollers.
Website is partially 'under construction'.

places.name: O Ya

famous.why: Char-crusted slabs of A5 beef with potato, the decadent cooked course (also offered as an add-on striploin with frites).

famous.item: Fried Kumamoto oyster with squid ink bubbles
famous.why: A long-running signature: a fried oyster topped with yuzu aioli and squid-ink 'bubbles', the bite people remember.
Pristine bluefin served as nigiri or seared tataki; critics describe it bursting with ponzu.
Tim Cushman's original signature, on the menu since the 2007 opening.
Seared foie gras on rice with sweet-savory glaze; a famous luxury bite.

tips: Book exactly 30 days out on OpenTable; note every allergy when booking, since the menu is composed in advance.
Ask for the counter to watch the sushi chefs (requests honored when possible, not guaranteed).
Supplemental courses (e.g., extra Wagyu) and a sake pairing can be added at the table, billed at the end.
Turning 20 in March 2027; watch the site/newsletter for anniversary dinners.

difficulty.why: Prepaid ~$383/person keeps demand manageable; weekend prime slots go within days of the 30-day release, parties over 4 need a phone call.

warnings: Very expensive and prepaid; non-refundable (transfer only).
Setlist changes nightly; specific signatures (oyster, hamachi, foie gras) are not guaranteed.
No BYOB, few spirits (sake/wine-focused); closed Sunday and Monday.
Small room; seating type (counter vs banquette) not guaranteed.

places.name: Tonino

famous.why: Little pasta pockets filled with warm, melting taleggio and finished with aged balsamic; the most-cited pasta.

famous.item: Countneck clams with guanciale and Calabrian chili
famous.why: Clams in a spicy, porky broth you'll want to mop up with pizza bianca.

evidence.source: Resy blog (How to Get Into Tonino)

famous.why: Light, chewy Roman flatbread you customize with add-ons like ricotta and hot honey or eggplant caponata.

evidence.source: Resy blog (How to Get Into Tonino)

famous.why: Eater says not to leave without a bowl of it.

famous.item: Mortadella with pecorino and house pickles
famous.why: The GM's pick and the restaurant's own 'must' order; a generous plate meant to share.

evidence.source: Resy blog (How to Get Into Tonino)

tips: Be at Resy at noon exactly 30 days out; otherwise set Notify, especially for the week before your date.
Walk-in: be one of the first two at the door at 5 PM for the counter seats; wait at Jadu (wine), Casa Verde (cocktails) or Galway House (beer) if you join the list.
The two counter seats in the back look into the open kitchen (Infatuation's favorite seat).
Parking: Centre St fills up; use the free municipal lot behind Casa Verde one block away.

difficulty.why: Only 28 seats; Resy says tables fill almost immediately after the noon release, and walk-ins get just two counter seats.

warnings: Closed Tuesday and Wednesday.
Tiny room; not suited to large groups.
Menu dated 10/2/26; small plates rotate seasonally.

places.name: Urban Hearth

famous.why: Eight to twelve seasonal courses served by the cooks at a six-seat counter; every critic calls it the move.

famous.item: Laminated buttermilk biscuit with smoked maple miso butter
famous.why: Flaky, buttery layered biscuit with a smoky-sweet miso butter; a cheap, perennial must-order on the a la carte menu.
A tiny savory cone of lobster with crème fraîche gelato, optionally topped with caviar.

famous.item: Savory-sweet cocktails and zero-proof drinks (e.g., Beach Rose, Low Light)
famous.why: Inventive drinks that swing between sweet and savory, including a shiso-nori zero-proof.

tips: For the full experience book the Chef's Counter (5:45 or 8:15 PM); note vegetarian or dietary needs in the reservation.
Bar & Salon takes walk-ins until 11 PM for biscuits, oysters and cocktails.
Order the biscuit and lobster cornette as starters even if you go a la carte.

difficulty.why: Six-seat counter books up ahead on weekends, but the larger new dining room and walk-in bar make a la carte tables easier.

warnings: Many listings (Eater, Time Out) still show the old Mass Ave / Davis-area address; it is now at 1281 Cambridge St in Inman Square.
Menu changes with the season; drinks named by critics may be gone.
Closed Monday; counter tasting only Tue-Sat.

places.name: 311 Omakase

famous.why: Chef Wei Fa Chen's tightly sourced progression (much of the fish flown from Japan) that earned a Michelin star; the nigiri run is the heart of the meal.
Tilefish fried so its scales go crisp, served with a light dashi; both critics call it a highlight when it's on.

famous.item: Uni and caviar in a shell-shaped wafer
famous.why: Sea urchin topped with caviar inside an airy, shell-like crisp; a luxurious one-biter.

tips: Be on Tock at noon ET on the 15th; a whole month's dates (75 days out) drop at once.
Join the Tock waitlist for multiple nights; cancellations surface close to the date.
Send any allergy info at least 72 hours ahead or it can't be accommodated.

difficulty.why: Michelin-starred, roughly 10 seats and two seatings a night; Eater and Infatuation both call it one of Boston's toughest reservations.

warnings: Very expensive: roughly $250-280 per person before drinks/tip (price reported differently by Eater and Infatuation).
No vegetarian, no-raw-fish or halal accommodations.
Courses change with the market; tilefish and uni bites are not guaranteed.
Search engines also surface an unrelated '311 Omakase'-style listing in North Cambridge; this is the South End brownstone at 605 Tremont.

places.name: Oleana

famous.why: The house signature since opening: a tall torched-meringue dome over coconut ice cream on a macaroon base, with passion fruit caramel.

evidence.source: Resy blog (Resy x Beli Boston list)

famous.item: Whipped Feta with Sweet & Hot Peppers
famous.why: Airy, tangy feta dip with a pepper kick, scooped with the house seeded crackers; the standard opener.

famous.item: Lemon Chicken with Za'atar & Turkish Cheese Pancake
famous.why: A deboned half chicken, stuffed with lemon confit and seared crisp, set on a crunchy cheese pancake.

famous.item: Chef's Choice Vegetable Meze & Dessert tasting
famous.why: The returned chef's-choice vegetarian tasting ($75/pp on the current menu) is the way to see the kitchen's range.

tips: Ask for the garden patio in warm months; it is one of Boston's most coveted and is walk-in only.
Order the baked Alaska early in the meal if the table is set on it; it is the dessert most tables come for.
The menu is largely vegetable meze; mixing 4-5 meze with one meat or fish plate is the usual move for two.
Walk-ins: arrive at opening for the held walk-in tables or the bar.

difficulty.why: Prime weekend times on Resy go well ahead within the 30-day window, but tables are held nightly for walk-ins and the bar/patio are unreservable.

warnings: Menu is seasonal; whipped feta, lemon chicken and baked Alaska are long-running but individual meze rotate.
Interior is dated per recent reviews; the patio is the draw.
Large parties (7+) are limited to early/late seatings and a fixed family-style menu.

places.name: Giulia

famous.why: The long-running house pasta: wide ribbons with a rich boar braise (currently with juniper and black trumpets).
A classic done right, loaded with house-cured pancetta in roughly equal measure to the noodles.
The bread is a vehicle for the savory bean crema and toppings that come with it; the version changes seasonally.
Gianduja-rich chocolate cake with roasted banana malt gelato; reads like an upscale banana split.

tips: Set an alarm for 10:00 AM ET exactly 14 days before your date; that is when OpenTable releases tables.
No luck? The 18-seat bar is walk-in with the full menu; arrive before the 5:30 open and put your name on the in-person list.
Order several pastas to share; the waitstaff will course them out for the table.
Big group (up to 12)? Book the Pasta Table, where the pasta is rolled by day, up to 6 months ahead for a family-style tasting.

difficulty.why: Small room, only a 2-week booking window, and it is typically fully reserved before opening; bar walk-ins are the realistic fallback.

warnings: Pastas rotate frequently; the wild boar pappardelle is a near-constant but toppings change with the season.
2-hour table limit; $25/person no-show fee.
Parties of 6 are rarely accepted in the main room.
Closed Thanksgiving (Nov 26, 2026).

places.name: Pammy's

famous.why: The unofficial signature: snail-shell pasta in a bolognese spiked with Korean chili paste for a sweet, slow heat.

evidence.source: The Boston Globe (quoted on the restaurant's site)

famous.why: A big, rich, garlicky cutlet that regulars treat as the main-course anchor.
A savory lobster small plate singled out for sharing at the communal table.
A recent pasta highlight cited in the 2026 Top 50 write-up; shows the seasonal pasta side of the menu.

tips: Want a la carte or a quick bite? Skip the reservation and walk in for the marble bar or lounge.
On the prix fixe you can pick any three courses, including all pastas if you like.
Ask for a table by the double-sided fireplace in winter, or the flower-lined communal table for a lively night.

difficulty.why: Prime weekend tables go within the 30-day window, but the bar/lounge holds walk-in space nightly.

warnings: Dining room is prix fixe only ($88/pp before drinks).
No reservations for groups larger than 5.
Menu changes often; seasonal dishes may not return. The lumache is the most consistent.

places.name: Moëca

famous.why: A big craggy fried monkfish fillet with sesame and a tamarind hot sauce; the dish critics keep pointing to, and on the current menu.
Spreadable, chili-spiked tuna riff on the Calabrian sausage, on jet-black toast; a signature share plate.
Breaded swordfish cutlet with chicories and a yogurt gribiche; pictured in the 2026 Top 50.
Scallop skirts stand in for tripe in a Roman-style tomato sauce, now served with cavatelli; a clever zero-waste dish.
Critics single out the desserts; the gelato is the recommended finish.

tips: Menu is posted daily by 4:30 PM on the site; check it before you go.
Plan on 2-3 raw-bar/share plates per person plus one large plate for the table.
If Giulia is booked, Moëca (same owners, around the corner) is often easier and shares the pasta skill.

difficulty.why: Popular and well reviewed but generally easier to book than sibling Giulia; groups of 5+ must go through phone/email.

warnings: Menu changes often (sometimes nightly); any dish may be off on a given night.
Closed Sunday and Monday (Tue-Sat per Time Out); last reservation 9 PM.
Very seafood-centric; limited options for non-fish eaters.

places.name: Lenox Sophia

famous.why: House tagliatelle finished in butter and olive oil with aged Parmigiano and shaved truffle; the dish both critics remember.
Crisp-bottomed black rice with seafood and a smoky aioli; a version (with green crab) is on the November 2026 menu.

famous.item: Buttermilk Fried Quail with nori-wasabi seasoning
famous.why: A playful Japanese-seasoned fried bird that shows the kitchen's mash-up style.
Plain-looking but packed with fermented-garlic, miso and umeboshi depth; the critic's standout.

tips: It's BYOB (wine/beer only, max 750 ml wine or 64 oz beer per person, sealed bottles); Social Wines is on the corner. No decanting or chilling service.
Ask for one of the 4 counter seats facing the open kitchen for the show.
Choose omnivore or vegetarian menu at booking; vegetarians are well served, but vegans, celiac and allium allergies cannot be accommodated.
Call if running late: tables are released after 15 minutes.

difficulty.why: Only 16 seats, 4 nights a week, and recurring top-list/James Beard semifinalist attention; book on Resy as soon as dates open.

warnings: Prix fixe only; dishes change seasonally, so individual items named in reviews may not be on.
Cannot accommodate celiac, allium allergies; limited for vegans and shellfish allergies.
$50/person late-cancel/no-show fee; 90-minute table limit.
No kids' menu or high chairs.

places.name: Spoke Wine Bar

famous.why: Savory little sunchoke doughnuts with aged/XO gouda and leek powder; the one perennial on an otherwise rotating menu.

famous.item: Griddled Chickpea Tempeh with maple vinegar
famous.why: A vegan plate that eats like chicken tenders with honey mustard; cited as an example of the kitchen's cleverness.

famous.item: Grilled Clam Skewers with coconut-chowder glaze
famous.why: A chowder-inspired grilled clam bite; an example of the menu's global-meets-New-England play.
The bar program (e.g. vermouth-driven drinks with 'secrets', fermented plantain, habanada) gets as much praise as the wine list.

tips: Always order the sunchoke donuts; build the rest from 3-4 small plates for two.
Ask staff for by-the-glass picks from lesser-known regions; the list is the point.
Weeknights are good for walk-ins at the bar; book weekends on Resy.
Same team opened Liars in Teele Square (2026) if Spoke is full.

difficulty.why: Small room and top-list status fill weekends, but it is open only Wed-Sat and weeknight walk-ins usually work.

warnings: Menu is seasonal and changes often; except the sunchoke donuts, named dishes may not be on.
Only open Wednesday-Saturday.
Tiny, tight space; not ideal for big groups.

places.name: Dalia

famous.why: Cooked by a dedicated three-person paella team at the central station; chicken, chorizo and shellfish over deeply savory rice, in two sizes.

famous.item: Ibérico Pluma with passionfruit caramel & quince
famous.why: Fire-grilled Ibérico pork with a fruity-sour caramel; a centerpiece of the wood-fired mains since opening.
Squid cut like noodles with sobrasada and almonds in a Sichuan-style sauce; the dish that sums up Dixon's Spain-as-a-starting-point approach.
Yellowtail layered with thin fig slices and a sherry-based ponzu; a crudo that feels new.

famous.item: Txistorra 'Hot Dog' and Anchoa y Mantequilla
famous.why: The snack picks: a Basque chorizo 'hot dog' and anchovies with charred-onion-ash butter, best with sangria or txakoli.

tips: Sit where you can watch the paella station and Josper grills under the skylight.
Share a small Valencia paella for two plus 2-3 tapas; paella comes in two sizes.
Finish with a sherry (e.g. palo cortado) or the passion-fruit 'copa' parfait.
Downstairs Leopard Lounge (21+) is the late-night cocktail option.

difficulty.why: Big, buzzy space with late hours helps, but NYT 50-best and many 2026 best-new lists make prime weekend times competitive.

warnings: Dress code: no athletic wear, overly revealing or sheer clothing.
No outside wine (no corkage); $5/person cake-cutting fee.
Socarrat (crispy bottom) on the paella is inconsistent per reviews.
Loud, scene-y room; skews younger crowd.

places.name: Bar Vlaha

famous.why: Charcoal spit-roasted lamb leg with garlic and rosemary; the centerpiece.

famous.item: House sourdough with spreads (taramosalata, kopanisti, etc.)
famous.why: Village-style sourdough with sheep's-milk butter and a trio of dips; how every meal should start.
Daily meat and vegetable pies, e.g., kreatopita and cornmeal-crust greens pie.
Roasted-then-fried oyster mushrooms with parsley spread.
House pork-and-fennel sausage with mustard yogurt.

tips: Start with bread plus three or six spreads, then share a grilled or spit-roasted meat.
Ask for the long table facing the open kitchen and charcoal spits.
Greek wine list leans to rare northern/central Greek bottles.
Large groups: the 'Giorti' feast platter covers lamb, chops, chicken and sausage.

difficulty.why: Infatuation calls it one of the toughest reservations in town; prime slots need about a month's notice.

warnings: Smoky room; clothes will smell of charcoal.
Daily pies and game specials rotate.

places.name: Wa Shin

famous.why: Chef Sky Zheng (trained under Daisuke Nakazawa) walks the counter through seasonal zensai then a run of mostly Japan-sourced nigiri; the meal itself is the draw.

evidence.source: Resy blog (Resy x Beli Boston list)

famous.why: Imported sea urchin is a highlight of the nigiri run, sometimes as a gunkan, sometimes layered over other fish.
Named alongside uni as one of the prized Japanese imports in the sequence.
A strong sake program built to pair with the omakase.

tips: Be on Resy at 12:00 PM ET exactly 14 days before your date; four seatings a night means few seats.
Arrive on time: seatings are fixed and the counter starts together.
Max party size online is 4; a two-top is easiest to land.

difficulty.why: Small counter, fixed seatings, 14-day release, and Michelin/top-list attention mean prime slots go fast.

warnings: Fixed omakase only; fish changes with the season, so specific pieces vary.
Mandatory 20% administrative fee on every check.
Parties over 4 must arrange by email; no online booking.
Expensive: one of Boston's priciest meals with sake.

places.name: Kaia

famous.why: A for-the-table island classic: a whole lobster over pasta in a brown butter and Metaxa brandy sauce.
Market-priced whole fish grilled simply and dressed with ladolemono; the anchor of the menu.
Yogurt-dressed hamachi with Asian accents; the NYT singled it out, and a version is on the current raw menu.
A deconstructed gyro with crispy meat and soft pita, ordered whole or half (now a crispy pork shoulder version).
Delicate cod cheeks in a smoked egg-lemon sauce; called one of the best cod dishes the critic had eaten.

tips: Come with a group and share: raw bar, several meze, then a whole fish or the lobster pasta for the table.
Try walking in for the 24-seat bar, which runs until 1 AM.
Patio season is the scene in warm months.
The wine list is entirely Aegean and all by the glass; ask for the small-production picks.

difficulty.why: NYT/Eater/BM attention keeps weekends busy, but it is a 100-seat room with walk-in space and a big bar.

warnings: Menu rotates seasonally; cod cheeks and the NYT-praised bingsu are not on the current (late 2026) menu.
Loud, music-forward dining room.
Closed Sunday and Monday.
Whole fish and lobster are market priced and can push the bill up quickly.

places.name: Celeste

famous.item: Ceviche (mixed seafood or blue cod, leche de tigre)
famous.why: Peruvian-style ceviche with a short, sharp marinade and big chunks of blue cod (the mixto adds squid and shrimp); the natural opener.
Wok-fired sirloin with tomato, onion and soy over rice, with a tangy edge; the hearty main most tables order.

famous.item: Pisco cocktails (pisco sour and house pisco drinks)
famous.why: The bar is built around pisco and mezcal; the frothy sours and the purple pisco drink are part of the fun.
Slow-cooked cilantro lamb stew with creamy canary beans and rice; the cold-night order.

famous.item: Scallops con Pasta a la Huancaína
famous.why: Seared scallops over squid-ink fettuccine in a fruity aji amarillo cream sauce.

tips: Go with 3-4 people so you can share a ceviche, a causa and two entrees.
Start with ceviche and take your time before ordering mains.
Watch the flames from the open kitchen; seats near it are the most fun.
If Celeste is full, sister restaurant La Royal in Cambridge is a strong backup.

difficulty.why: Tiny and always buzzing; reserve on OpenTable for weekends, though weeknight bar walk-ins are often possible.

warnings: Small, loud, high-energy room; can feel chaotic.
Daily specials rotate; check the posted daily menu.

places.name: Jahunger

famous.why: The namesake plate: thick hand-pulled noodles stir-fried with marinated beef, chives and onion - the dish every review points to first.
Chewy Xinjiang rice noodles tossed with ground chicken; a regulars' favorite.
The classic Uyghur pulled-noodle dish topped with a stir-fry of meat and vegetables - Michelin calls out the pulled noodles as the specialty.
Chilled chicken appetizer glossed in a secret chili sauce with onion, black fungus and scallion - a fan favorite starter.
Small marinated lamb skewers crusted with cumin and pepper.

tips: Start with the hand-made lamb dumplings or samsa, then split two noodle dishes for the table.
Blistered green beans are the go-to vegetable foil; a can of Wang Lao Ji herbal tea helps tame the heat.
Big Plate Chicken (Chicken Stew, ~$34) is a shareable centerpiece for groups.
Weekend lunch (Sat/Sun from noon) is the easiest time to walk in.
Vegetarians: Spicy Tiger (blistered eggplant), stir-fried beans, eggplant laghman.

difficulty.why: Casual walk-in noodle house; possible short waits on weekend evenings.

warnings: Much of the menu is genuinely spicy - ask for milder heat if sensitive.
Closed Mondays.
No online reservations.

places.name: Sumiao Hunan Kitchen

famous.why: Farmhouse-style stir-fry of thick-cut pork belly with long horn peppers and garlic - the classic Hunan home-cooking dish here, with real heat.
Pan-fried pork potstickers done simply and precisely - the easy crowd-pleasing starter.
Hand-torn cabbage wok-charred with dried chilis, aged vinegar and garlic until it eats almost meaty - the standout vegetable.
Thick white fish fillets steamed under a pickled-chili and garlic sauce; called a must for the table.
Hometown-style stir-fried beef with pickled yellow peppers, ginger and cilantro - bright, sour-spicy Hunan flavor.

tips: Order family-style; the restaurant itself recommends sharing.
Pair a spicy wok dish with a cooling vegetable (Shaoshan cabbage, string beans) and rice - rice is ordered separately.
Weekday lunch (Tue-Fri) has a fixed-price entree menu that is the best value.
Patio seating in warm months; live band nights listed on the site.
Dry-fried string beans with peppercorn oil are another strong vegetable side.

difficulty.why: Large Kendall room with Resy availability most nights; weekends book up modestly.

warnings: Many dishes cannot be made non-spicy (marked on the menu).
Table time limits (1.5-2 hrs).
Closed Mondays.
Auto 20% gratuity + 3% kitchen fee for parties of 7+.

places.name: Brassica Kitchen + Café

famous.why: Chicken brined for days in the leftover ferment from the house hot sauce, then fried - one of the restaurant's most popular plates since opening; add a house hot sauce.

evidence.source: Boston.com / Boston Globe Media (What to order)
Phantom Gourmet / CBS Boston (crispy chicken sandwich, 2017)

famous.why: Crispy fried Brussels sprouts dressed with maple, umeboshi, miso and lemon - a signature since the pop-up days.

evidence.source: Boston.com / Boston Globe Media (What to order)

famous.why: Earthy-sweet risotto cooked in a Parmesan-rind broth with house koji - the dish the chef says best sums up the kitchen.

evidence.source: Boston.com / Boston Globe Media (What to order)

famous.why: Moules done with Thai curry flavors and a rotating starch for dipping; a cold-weather fixture regulars wait for.

evidence.source: Boston.com / Boston Globe Media (What to order)

tips: 'The Ride' chef's tasting menu (~$100/pp incl. tax & tip, 2-person min; can be pescatarian) is the easy way to try everything.
Take home a bottle of the house hot sauces (carrot habanero, blueberry pasilla, etc.).
Weekend brunch is a neighborhood favorite - diners rave about biscuits & gravy and brown-butter pancakes.
Also serves Detroit- and Roman-style pizzas at dinner.
Daytime café for coffee and house donuts; steps from Forest Hills Orange Line.

difficulty.why: Neighborhood spot with OpenTable availability on most nights; weekend brunch is busiest.

warnings: Closed Mondays and Tuesdays.
Menu changes often - the Globe-praised bluefin crudo is not on the Nov 2026 menu (hamachi crudo instead); mussels are seasonal.
Service model: site describes a 20% admin + 3% benefits fee in lieu of tipping; current dinner menu says prices include tax and gratuity - check your bill, don't double tip.

places.name: Fallow Kin

famous.item: Squid (stuffed Rhode Island squid / squid Milanese)
famous.why: The kitchen's signature use of the whole squid - pounded and fried crisp, or stuffed - with bright chile and citrus accents; both major reviews singled out a squid dish.
Crisp-skinned, brick-pressed local chicken - the classic main that recurs across seasons.
A wagyu burger with cheddar sauce and giardiniera on a sesame potato bun, nodding to the beloved burger of Craigie on Main, which used to occupy the space.
The must-order cocktail; comes in a full or a playful half-size pour.

famous.item: Bread: Hazlet rye sourdough & laminated brioche
famous.why: Thick-cut house rye sourdough (with apple butter) and honey-buttered brioche - an easy table opener the Globe called out.

tips: First visit: let the staff steer the order and pacing (Time Out's advice).
Book the Chef's Counter for the full 7-course experience; the dining room is a la carte.
Save room for dessert - reviewers rate the desserts and house ice creams among the best things here.
Try the Fallow Kin trousseau gris made for the restaurant by Jolie-Laide.

difficulty.why: Globe 4-star review and Resy Hit List buzz make prime weekend tables and Chef's Counter seats go fast; weeknights are easier.

warnings: Menu is hyper-seasonal - the squid dishes are not on the Nov 2026 main menu, and the burger is a bar-menu item that may rotate.
Closed Tuesdays.
Bright, white-lit dining room - not a dim, candlelit vibe.

places.name: Grill 23 & Bar

famous.why: An 18-oz prime ribeye dry-aged for 100 days and seared under an ultra-hot broiler - funky, tender and the house showpiece.
The dependable classic cut; the Infatuation calls it a strong pick even next to the splurge cuts. A dry-aged version is also offered.
Japanese A5 wagyu, sold as a small tasting add-on or a 6-oz steak - one of the best bites the Infatuation reviewer had in recent memory.
Towering platter of shrimp, oysters, lobster tail, crab and salmon tartare - the celebratory start.
Long-running tall coconut layer cake the menu itself bills as 'famous'; frequently praised by diners.

tips: Ask for an ice-cold martini - the Infatuation highlights them.
Chef-recommended sides with the ribeye: taleggio creamed spinach and the truffle Grill 23 tots.
Upstairs/downstairs rooms: request a secluded table for occasions, or eat at the clubby bar.
Grand Award-winning wine list - worth asking the sommelier.
Steaks are also sold raw through the Grill 23 butcher shop.

difficulty.why: Large two-level room with good OpenTable availability, but prime weekend and holiday times (December, NYE) fill well ahead.

warnings: Very expensive: steaks ~$79-$325, sides $16-$22 a la carte.
Dressy, old-school steakhouse atmosphere; can be loud on busy nights.

places.name: Puritan & Company

famous.why: Buttery, salt-flecked house rolls served warm with cultured butter - widely called the best version in town; order them every time.
Soft house-made cavatelli with lots of sweet crab in a light lemony broth - the signature pasta.
Plump shrimp in a deep black-garlic sauce under fried shallots - save a roll to mop it up.
House orecchiette carrying a rich pork-and-beef ragu; one of the reliable pastas.
Local oysters with cucumber mignonette - a recommended opener, and half price 5-6 PM.

tips: Rolls come two per order - get one order per two people at least.
Seafood towers (Neighborhood ~$50 / Cantabrigian ~$120) for groups.
Five-course chef's tasting (~$85; whole table must participate) with optional wine pairing.
After dinner, go next door to Puritan Oyster Bar for an amaro and dessert; its swordfish pastrami and lobster toast get raves.
Much produce comes from the chef-owner's family farm in Groton - lean into the vegetable plates.

difficulty.why: Established neighborhood restaurant with OpenTable availability and walk-ins welcome; weekend prime time books up a few days out.

warnings: Crab cavatelli and garlic shrimp are not on the Nov 2026 posted dinner menu - seasonal menu; may not be available.
Metered street parking until 6 PM; Windsor lot nearby.

places.name: Somaek

famous.why: Hot, juicy steamed dumplings with a thicker, homestyle wrapper - repeatedly called a must-order.
Cold buckwheat noodles in sweet-spicy gochujang with cucumber, gim and a soft egg - soothing and bright.
Spicy-sweet gochujang pork bulgogi with rice - the main staff steer people toward.
Soybean-paste stew with pork, clams, tofu and potato - quietly deep and comforting.
The namesake soju-and-beer mix; pair it with a Korean-forward list of soju, makgeolli and yakju.

tips: Every meal comes with three free banchan (mu radish kimchi and soy-braised beef are standouts); extras cost more.
Order several small plates family-style - dishes come out as ready, not in courses.
Two can usually snag bar seats on a weeknight without a reservation.
Chef Jamie Bissonnette's Temple Records bar (sushi/listening bar) is in the same building for after dinner.
Michelin Guide recommended (2025).

difficulty.why: Popular, Michelin-recommended, modest-size room; prime weekend tables need a few days' notice but the bar is walk-in friendly.

warnings: Closed Sundays.
$25/pp no-show / late-cancel fee.
Mandu fillings rotate: the Nov 2026 menu lists steamed beef & scallion and fried mushroom-tofu, not the pork-kimchi version early reviews describe.
At least one diner felt the bill (~$65pp) ran high for the portions.

places.name: Via Cannuccia

famous.why: Long Roman paddle-baked pizzas with an airy crust; reviewers push the white pies (mortadella-burrata-pistachio, quattro formaggi) and the sausage pie for the table.
Roman fried risotto balls, crunchy outside and molten-cheesy within, served over a Romano cream - worth the trip on their own.
Sardinian pasta that rotates sauces (most recently sausage with broccoli crema) - order it whenever it appears.
Morning croissants, danishes and rotating Italian pastries baked in-house for the weekend brunch crowd.

tips: Check the chalkboard specials - seasonal dishes change almost daily.
Current menu (Nov 2026) includes Tonnarello cacio e pepe, Pacchero alla Genovese (short-rib ragu) and chef Stefano's house porchetta.
Lots of seafood: mussels, octopus salad, fettuccine alla pescatora.
Weekend brunch 9-2 is the easier way in; arrive early for pastries.
Ranked in Boston Magazine's Top 50 Restaurants (2025). A bakery/wine-bar offshoot, Bottega Cannuccia, is planned for Fields Corner.

difficulty.why: Tiny ~40-seat room, industry favorite, and described by the Globe (Aug 2026) as one of the city's toughest tables; book on OpenTable well ahead.

warnings: Closed Tuesdays.
Strict table time limits (1.5-2 hrs).
Menu rotates: on the Nov 2026 dinner menu the supplì are taleggio-spinach, not cacio e pepe, and gnocchetti are not listed.
Small kitchen - dishes may arrive at different times.

places.name: Woods Hill Pier 4

famous.why: Towering raw-bar platter (oysters, clams, Old Bay-aioli mussels, lobster and crab salads, shrimp, crudo) built to go with the harbor view.
Fresh lobster salad stuffed into a warm popover - a brunch-only riff on the lobster roll with near-celebrity status around town.
A menu staple: charred broccoli with cheddar and smoked-garlic aioli and crispy leeks.
House-made bucatini with house-cured guanciale; one of the recurring pasta staples.
Smoky signature margarita; the cocktail program is a highlight.

tips: Brunch on a sunny day in a window booth is the classic move; order the popover and the Cubano.
Most meat, produce and dairy come from The Farm at Woods Hill in Bath, NH - the meat dishes are a strength.
Save room for dessert or the espresso martini.
Pier 4 Caviar Service comes with warm popovers.
Big patio in warm months; Michelin Guide selected (2025).

difficulty.why: Large room with Resy availability, but weekend brunch, patio season and sunset tables fill up.

warnings: Lobster popover and Cubano are brunch-only (Sat-Sun).
Pricey: lobster popover ~$43, shellfish tower ~$138.
Menu changes seasonally.
No parking validation at nearby garages.

places.name: La Royal

famous.why: Bracing Lima-style ceviche (blue cod or mixto) and its 'tiger's milk' shot, served in cut-glass stemware - the place to start.
Whole branzino grilled in plantain leaves with Amazonian seasonings, onions and peppers - Resy's 'don't miss' and an Infatuation favorite.
The house pisco sour, tinted fuchsia with hibiscus-and-pomegranate-infused pisco - the signature cocktail.
Chifa classic of wok-seared sirloin with tomato, onion and soy - a savory umami bomb.
Nikkei-style 'sashimi' of thin portobello slices in a gingery soy dressing - a great vegetarian starter.

tips: Copper bar is good for solo diners and cocktail-first visits; walk-ins welcome.
Chifa dishes (marked * on the menu) reflect the chef's own Chinese-Peruvian heritage - pescado con verduras with house XO sauce is another strong pick.
Pisco Martini (horseradish pisco) and Margarita Morada (purple-corn mezcal) are fun alternates.
Sister restaurant to Celeste in Somerville.

difficulty.why: Neighborhood spot, open nightly, OpenTable availability and walk-ins welcome; weekend prime time can fill.

warnings: Gratineed scallops (praised in reviews) are not on the Nov 2026 posted dinner menu.
Some dishes carry real aji heat.
Dinner only; a short drive or bus ride from Harvard Square.

places.name: Zurito

famous.why: Simple garlic-and-tomato toast that critics say you must top with the Cantabrian anchovies.
The classic Basque bar bite; the anchovy-forward pintxos are the house strength.
Hand-sliced Spanish hams (legs hang over the bar) with manchego and tomato honey.
Mini croissant stuffed with acorn-fed jamón ibérico paleta.
Steak tartare on toast with anchovy, olive and fried garlic; Infatuation called it a best-bite contender.

tips: Order several cheap pintxos first (most are single bites), then a ham-and-cheese board, then decide on raciones.
Ask for the anchovy add-on with the pan con tomate.
Spanish-focused wine list (Wine Spectator Award of Excellence); by-the-glass Spanish reds are the value play.
Bar and standing counter up front are livelier; the back dining room is darker and quieter.
Big-group splurge: the 32 oz bone-in txuleton ribeye.

difficulty.why: Only about 60 seats and a hot Beacon Hill opening; prime weekend slots go fast on the 30-day Resy release, but bar/high-top seats help.

warnings: Pintxos are small and priced per piece; the bill adds up quickly.
Patio is seasonal (closing party held mid-Nov 2026).

places.name: Hecate

famous.item: Signature cocktails from the current 'book of spells' volume
famous.why: Rotating volumes of ingredient-heavy, theatrical cocktails in unusual glassware; Vol. VI (late 2026) includes She of the Night, Fasnacht and Hollow Hills.

famous.item: Bar snacks (stuffed dates, fried chicken, chickpea fritters)
famous.why: A short snack list built to soak up the drinks.

tips: Arrive 30 minutes before opening to skip the wait.
Tell the bartenders ('spirit guides') what you like; ordering a basic highball is frowned on.
There's also a zero-proof list.
Entrance is a door in the public alley behind Gloucester St, not on Newbury.

difficulty.why: Walk-in only with about 24 seats; waits of up to two hours reported on busy nights.

warnings: No reservations, no phone.
Closed Sunday and Monday.
Cocktails are pricey (around 20 dollars) and the named drinks change with each menu volume; older-volume drinks (Snake Oil, Dragon Gate) are gone.
Do not contact Krasi about Hecate.

places.name: Yvonne's

famous.why: Labor-intensive layered potato cubes with joppiesaus and gouda; the dish reviewers lead with.
Shareable mules best ordered in the book-lined Library Bar.
Feast-for-two centerpiece of seared tuna over fregola.
Social-plate meatballs with Chinese garlic sauce and spicy peanuts.

tips: Entrance is through a faux hair salon off Winter Place.
Order about two plates per person and share.
Have drinks in the Library Bar; The Gallery private room hides behind a bookcase.
Good late-night option: open until 1-2 AM.

difficulty.why: Large multi-room venue; SevenRooms usually has tables, especially early or late.

warnings: Food reviews are mixed versus the spectacular room.
Popcorn brûlée and stone-fired pitas from older reviews are not on the Nov 2026 menu.
Gets loud and clubby later at night.

places.name: haley.henry

famous.why: Imported tins (sardines, mackerel, octopus) opened tableside on a slate with chips and garnishes.

famous.item: Natural wine by the glass / half bottle
famous.why: James Beard-semifinalist list of small, often women-made natural wines; most bottles available as halves.
Daily raw-fish plates, e.g., black bass ceviche with coconut and honey.
Simple buttery crab toast that Time Out calls a standout.
Themed gourmet hot dogs every Wednesday.

tips: Ask the bartender what they're excited about; staff picks are reliable.
Half bottles let two people try more wines.
Check the events calendar for theme nights (wine-country nights, Pride parties).
Sidewalk seating expands capacity in warm months.

difficulty.why: Small but mostly walk-in bar seating plus Resy tables; waits only at peak weekend hours.

warnings: Tiny space with limited seating.
Closed Sundays and Mondays.
Crudo, ceviche and tins rotate daily.

places.name: Backbar

famous.why: The list is rebuilt around a pop-culture theme every few months (Star Wars, animation studios, cryptids), with nerdy, inventive drinks.
An ever-changing clear milk punch is the house staple; the bar says it has made hundreds of versions.
Bartenders happily build a custom drink from your mood or preferred spirit.

tips: Arrive near opening (5 PM) on Fri/Sat to skip the hallway line.
If the menu reads too obscure, describe what you like and let the bartender riff.
Ask which clarified milk punch is on right now.

difficulty.why: Walk-in only, small room, weekend line.

warnings: Ownership changed: the Field & Vine team bought it in 2025 and cofounder Sam Treadway left at the end of 2025; menus/vibe may shift.
Official website domain is down (Wix error) as of Nov 2026; confirm hours on social media.
Specific themed drinks rotate every few months.

places.name: Blossom Bar

famous.why: The Sichuan Garden kitchen's tingly noodles are the go-to soak-up dish with the cocktails.
Award-winning signature of aged rum, passionfruit, coffee, cinnamon and mascarpone.
Opening-era papaya cocktail named for a Colombian beauty queen turned smuggler.

tips: Pair the tropical drinks with Sichuan dishes (dumplings in chili vinaigrette, kung pao).
Walk-in section exists; arrive at 5 PM on weekends or book Tock.
The 2026 menu leads with Palm Viper, Rosalia, Bae Bae Colada (ube) and Makrut Lime; ask if older classics can still be made.

difficulty.why: Buzzy and loud on weekends, but bookable on Tock with walk-in space.

warnings: Gloria and Angie Valencia are not on the current posted 2026 menu, so they may be retired; ask the bartender.
90-minute table limit for reservations.
Loud, energetic room.

places.name: Liars

famous.item: Beef tongue with peppers and cheese
famous.why: Tender tongue done like a sizzling cheesesteak; both reviewers called it the standout.

famous.item: Griddled corn muffin with blueberry ice cream
famous.why: Buttery, hot griddled muffin topped with a scoop of blueberry ice cream.
Tuna meatballs in spicy tomato sauce that the Globe called brilliant.
Smoky-sweet cold terrine with carrot ribbons; a server favorite.
Mango distillate, pineapple rum, purple rice and sparkling wine; the Infatuation's favorite cocktail.

tips: Get the mixed-grain rice with crab butter on the side; Infatuation says it lifts every dish.
Cocktails get playful garnishes (squirt guns, an olive frozen in ice for the Humor Me).
Ask the spirits team for a pour you've never had; the list leans on rare bottles.

difficulty.why: New (Aug 2026) and well reviewed; book on OpenTable for prime time, bar walk-ins possible.

warnings: Menu is seasonal and new; dishes may rotate.
Closed Sunday and Monday.
Non-alcoholic drinks are pricey for their size (Crimson).

places.name: Toro

famous.why: The signature: charred corn slathered in alioli, lime, espelette and aged cheese.
Big shareable pans of rice with shrimp, mussels, clams, chorizo and chicken.
Crisp fried potatoes with alioli and spicy tomato; you can upgrade to a 'brava bomb'.

famous.item: Pato con membrillo (smoked duck drumettes, quince)
famous.why: Quince-glazed duck drumsticks singled out as unforgettable.
Tomato-jam and pickled-onion sliders that Infatuation calls a house favorite.

tips: Order paella early: the menu asks for a minimum 30 minutes and it is dinner only.
A half order of corn works for two.
Bar seats face the open kitchen and are easiest to get without a booking.
Sunday brunch is back if dinner is booked out.

difficulty.why: Popular 20-year-old South End staple; prime tables need booking ahead but the bar takes walk-ins.

warnings: Loud, party-music atmosphere.
Older guides say Toro is walk-in only; it now takes reservations via OpenTable.
Seasonal menu; specific tapas rotate.

places.name: Fox & the Knife

famous.why: Warm focaccia oozing taleggio and mozzarella; the opener nearly every table gets.
Chef Akunowicz's own can't-miss pasta; hand-rolled ribbons with a rich ragù.
Cacio e pepe riff finished with goat butter and pink peppercorns.
Puffy fried dough draped with mortadella, a lighter alternative to the focaccia.
Charred broccoli starter with white miso, migas and colatura.

tips: Start with the focaccia (or gnocco fritto), then share pastas course by course.
Aperitivo snacks like fried chili chickpeas pair with the spritz list; there's an amaro program for after.
Bar seats are walk-in only; arrive at opening for the best shot.

difficulty.why: Michelin-recognized chef-driven spot; prime tables vanish soon after the rolling 30-day release.

warnings: Small plates and pastas add up; plan several per person.
Menu changes seasonally; whole fish and some pastas rotate.

places.name: Row 34

famous.item: Lobster roll (warm buttered or Ethel's creamy)
famous.why: Two styles from Jeremy Sewall's family recipes; the hot buttered one is the local favorite.
Island Creek lineage; dozens of East Coast oysters are the reason to come.
Beer-steamed mussels with bread for the broth; matches the strong beer list.
Rotating raw fish crudos (tuna with black garlic aioli was a highlight).

tips: Sit at the L-shaped bar and order oysters by the dozen with a beer.
Beer list is deep and rotating; cocktails use cordials (no full liquor license).
Lunch is quieter than dinner.
Lobster rolls are market price; ask before ordering.

difficulty.why: Busy and noisy most nights; typical waits for tables, but plenty of bar seats and OpenTable availability.

warnings: Loud room.
Lobster roll priced at market (MP), can be expensive.
Five Row 34 locations exist; this entry is the original Fort Point/Seaport one.

places.name: Baleia

famous.why: Head-on shrimp in a spicy beer-and-chili stew you'll want to drink.
Saffron rice with rich duck and chouriço; a heavy-hitting main.
Deconstructed caldo verde: cod over green sauce, crispy potato and smoky chouriço.
Golden pineapple-juice buns with chamomile butter; cheap and constantly flying out of the kitchen.
Opening signature: copper-pot stew of pork, clams, mussels and shrimp.

tips: Start with a white port tonic and an order of sweet rolls.
All-Portuguese wine list (about 70 bottles); port and Madeira by the glass with dessert.
Explorador tasting menu (per person) is an option for groups.
Desserts: pastéis de nata and sonhos (fried dough with port caramel).

difficulty.why: Big room in an out-of-the-way South End block; Resy usually has tables and the bar takes walk-ins.

warnings: Cataplana and bifana sliders are not on the Nov 2026 online menu; may be retired or seasonal.
Some reviewers find the dining room chilly near the entrance.

places.name: The Wig Shop

famous.why: Warm lobster in harissa butter on mini buttermilk pancakes with tobiko and dill.
Supercharged espresso-martini-style rum drink in a teacup with whipped cream and a chocolate pretzel; limited to one per guest.
Best-seller of citron vodka, raspberry and elderflower under glitter foam.
Tableside absinthe service for two, a Time Out tip.

tips: Book the 5-7 PM Resy window, or go Sun/Mon when reservations run all night.
Couch seating only, no bar stools.
Big Champagne list (30+ bottles) if celebrating.
Food is finger-food canapés; plan dinner elsewhere or order several.

difficulty.why: Small couch-only room; prime weekend hours are walk-in only.

warnings: Rise & Grind is one per person.
21+ with ID.
Cocktail menu rotates (current toy-themed 2026-27 book); signature drinks may change.

places.name: Farmacia

famous.why: Three to four bespoke cocktails from a quarterly themed menu, tailored after a chat about your tastes.
Small palate-cleansing bites and a dessert course built into the ticket.

tips: Set an alarm for noon on the 1st of the month, 60 days before your target date.
Tell the bartender your preferences up front; any drink can be adjusted.
Current menu (Nov 2026) is Chapter 20: Tales for the Longer Nights.

difficulty.why: Nine seats, prepaid tickets that sell out within minutes of release.

warnings: Drinks change every quarter, so pictured cocktails won't be on.
Prepaid and non-refundable style ticketing.
Brief placed it upstairs at Mare; sources describe it on North Square inside the All Day Hospitality (Ciao Roma/Mare) building.

places.name: Trina's Starlite Lounge

famous.item: Hot dogs (Starlite dog, corn dog, Hot Dog Tower)
famous.why: The bar's calling card ('hot dogs, High Lifes and hugs'); griddled dogs loaded with cheese, fries and slaw.
Top-tier brunch plate at the Sunday brunch.
Creamy Ritz-cracker-topped mac, add a hot dog if you like.
Infatuation's pick for weekend drinks; the house espresso martini.

tips: Weekly specials: Monday cantina, Tuesday spaghetti and meatball, Wednesday sloppy joe.
Brunch is Sundays from 11 AM; Monday industry brunch now appears limited to holiday Mondays per the menu.
Hot Dog Tower (5 dogs + fries) is the group order.

difficulty.why: Walk-in neighborhood bar; only brunch and late weekends get crowded.

warnings: No reservations.
Dark, loud dive atmosphere late at night.
Old domain trinastarlitelounge.com is parked; use trinastarlite.com.

places.name: The Koji Club

famous.why: 80-plus bottles with small 4 oz pours; staff taste you through styles until you find one you love.
Freshly milled Hokkaido rice with add-ons like furikake, miso, pickles, butter-tamari.
Chef Moe Kuroki (ex-Oisa Ramen) cooks a set family meal on Wednesday nights.
Sweet-tart cucumber pickles from the founder's mother's recipe.

tips: Sit at the bar and ask for tastes; no pressure to commit to a bottle.
Go Wednesday for makanai.
Weekend afternoons (Sat/Sun from 2 PM) are calmer and good on the patio.
Parking map is on the official site (Speedway lots).

difficulty.why: Walk-ins always welcome, though the tiny room fills on weekend nights.

warnings: Very small space.
Sake list is seasonal; featured bottles change.

places.name: Extra Dirty Cocktail Club

famous.why: Progressive cocktail courses with food equal to a full dinner, around a theme that changes a few times a year.
The namesake drink; the bar plays up souped-up martinis.
A creamy espresso martini singled out for sweet-tooth drinkers.

tips: Current theme (Nov 2026): Act 8, 'From Harvest to Hearth: A New England Story' (spiced carrot, pumpkin pie, corn & cheddar, apple & coffee).
Enter through The Red Fox and head behind the curtain.
Eat lightly beforehand; four courses of food are included.
Watch Instagram (@extradirtynorthend) for releases.

difficulty.why: 20 seats, prepaid tickets that go fast, walk-in only through a Tock waitlist.

warnings: Prepaid and final; no standing service.
Strict time limit (~110 min).
Menu changes with each Act; earlier-reported drinks may be gone.

places.name: Wusong Road

famous.why: Hand-folded daily with house cream cheese, notably light; the bar bills it as Boston's best.
Classic tiki mai tai built on house-made juices; often called a top version in town.
Old-school shareable bowl, done craft-style.
Rum infused with mango sticky rice, mango puree and lime; milky and tropical.

tips: Come for drinks plus rangoons rather than a full dinner; the food reviews are mixed beyond the hits.
Drinks come in collectible tiki mugs, which are sold as merch.
Pandan Express (gin, pandan, melon) is a lighter pick.

difficulty.why: Bookable on OpenTable with a big two-level space.

warnings: Food beyond the rangoons gets mixed reviews (Boston Magazine, Crimson).
Strong, sweet drinks.
Parking is hard while the municipal lot is closed.
